newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Albright ties aid to cooperation by Bosnia parties.
newsitem.headline: Albright ties aid to cooperation by Bosnia parties.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, visiting Bosnia, urged its former warring factions on Sunday to abide by a peace agreement or lose out on crucial reconstruction aid.

Albright, invoking the memory of America's Marshall Plan after World War Two, said Washington would extend aid to Bosnia as long as political leaders lived up to their promises under the 1995 Dayton peace accords.

"What is happening here in Sarajevo is the modern day version of a Marshall Plan where America provides assistance, but it provides assistance to those who help themselves," she told reporters in the Bosnian capital.
If Bosnian authorities failed to carry out projects devised "to knit the multi-ethnic society together, then there will not be American assistance," she said.

She held talks with Bosnian Moslem, Croat and Serb members of the collective presidency as part of a U.S. effort to bolster the 1995 peace agreement, which ended four years of war in former Yugoslavia.
Albright's visit coincided with growing international concern that the fragile peace is unravelling, only a year before the NATO-led peace force is due to withdraw.

NATO troops have separated rival armies but nationalist authorities are seeking to seal the results of wartime "ethnic cleansing" by discouraging reconciliation and blocking refugees from returning to their homes.
Albright flew by helicopter to the disputed northern town of Brcko, where U.S. troops are stationed in one of the country's most volatile flashpoints.
She planned to preside over a ceremony reopening an important bridge across the Sava river linking Bosnia with Croatia.
The northern border, which straddles Bosnia's autonomous Serb republic, has been closed or severely restricted since Croatia broke away from Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia in 1991.
Bosnian officials said they expected Croatia to agree this month to reopening several other border crossings along the Sava which they said would provide a major boost to trade.
In Sarajevo, Albright placed flowers on the Vrbanja bridge to mourn the war's first victim, Suada Dilberovic, who was cut down by sniper fire during a 1992 demonstration.

Albright chatted with children at a playground and took a stroll down the notorious former "Sniper's Alley" where Sarajevans once dashed across intersections during the nationalist Serb siege of the city.
"There is a great deal to be done but let us never forget that three years ago people were still dying on these streets and we would not be able to be taking these kind of walks," she said.

Albright flew to Bosnia a day after delivering stern warnings to leaders of Bosnia's powerful neighbours, Croatia and Serbia, who sought to carve up the country between them during the 1992-95 conflict.

In blunt language, Albright reprimanded presidents Franjo Tudjman of Croatia and Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia for failing to hand over indicted war criminals and dragging their feet on other key aspects of the U.S.-brokered peace agreement.
She called for Milosevic, a key signatory of the U.S.- brokered Dayton accords, to stop "stonewalling" and cooperate with the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

She said Milosevic needed to secure the extradition of former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, who still wields power in Serb-controlled territory from his offices in Pale, 16 km (10 miles) outside Sarajevo.
In the Croatian capital Zagreb, Albright said she told Tudjman that he must prevent violence against minority Serb war refugees trying to return to Croatia and to cooperate with the U.N. tribunal.

Albright said on Sunday that the continued presence of war crimes suspects in Bosnia represented "the major roadblock to progress" but offered no details about how Washington intended to resolve the problem.
"The United States is looking into options of how to strengthen the work of the war crimes tribunal. We do believe that getting the war criminals is a priority issue," she said.
